title: From layers to full architectures
text:
From layers to full architectures
Key idea
A CNN architecture is not just a list of convolutional layers. It is a structured
composition of:
• stem: early feature extraction from the raw image,
• stages: repeated blocks at different spatial resolutions,
• downsampling: reduce spatial size and increase semantic abstraction,
• head: convert features into task outputs.
Takeaway
Modern CNNs are designed around stages, blocks, and scaling rules, not
isolated layers.

title: Canonical CNN structure
text:
Canonical CNN structure
Typical classification pipeline
Image →Stem →Stage 1 →Stage 2 →Stage 3
→Stage 4 →Pooling →Classifier
Shape trend
(B, 3, H, W ) →(B, C1, H/4, W /4) →(B, C2, H/8, W /8)
→(B, C3, H/16, W /16) →(B, C4, H/32, W /32)
Takeaway
CNNs usually trade spatial resolution for semantic abstraction.
Note: This shape trend is a common pattern in many classification backbones, not a
universal rule for all CNN architectures.

Feature hierarchy in CNNs
Early stages
• High spatial resolution.
• Capture local patterns: edges, corners, colors, textures.
Middle stages
• Medium spatial resolution.
• Capture parts, repeated motifs, object components.
Late stages
• Low spatial resolution.
• Capture high-level semantic concepts.

title: Architecture design questions
text:
Architecture design questions
When designing or choosing a CNN
• How deep should the network be?
• How wide should each stage be?
• Where should downsampling happen?
• Which block should be repeated?
• How many parameters and FLOPs are acceptable?
• Is the target server, desktop GPU, mobile, or embedded device?
Takeaway
Architecture choice is a trade-off among accuracy, latency, memory, and
deployment constraints.

title: VGG: principle
text:
VGG: principle
Core design
VGG uses repeated small convolutions:
3 × 3 →3 × 3 →MaxPool
organized into several stages.
Design philosophy
• Use a simple and uniform architecture.
• Increase depth by stacking many 3 × 3 convolutions.
• Replace large kernels by multiple small kernels.
Takeaway
VGG is simple, clean, and useful for teaching, but computationally heavy.

title: VGG: strengths and cautions
text:
VGG: strengths and cautions
Strengths
• Very easy to understand.
• Good didactic architecture for hierarchical feature extraction.
• Useful baseline for explaining transfer learning.
Cautions
• Parameter-heavy, especially the fully connected classifier.
• Less efficient than ResNet, MobileNet, EfficientNet, and ConvNeXt.
• Usually not the best modern default for deployment.
Reference
Simonyan and Zisserman, Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale
Image Recognition, ICLR 2015.

title: ResNet: principle
text:
ResNet: principle
Problem
Very deep plain networks are difficult to optimize.
Core idea
Instead of learning a direct mapping H(x), a residual block learns:
F(x) = H(x) −x
so that:
y = F(x) + x
Takeaway
Residual connections make it easier to train deep networks by providing
shortcut paths for information and gradients.

title: ResNet: basic block

ResNet: basic block
Basic residual block
x →Conv →BN →ReLU →Conv →BN →+ x →ReLU
Shape requirement

F(x) ∈RB×C×H×W ,
x ∈RB×C×H×W
Takeaway
If shape changes, the shortcut path needs a projection, usually a 1 × 1
convolution.

title: ResNet: strengths and cautions
text:
ResNet: strengths and cautions
Strengths
• Strong default backbone.
• Widely used in classification, detection, segmentation, and retrieval.
• Many pretrained checkpoints available.
Cautions
• Deeper variants may overfit small datasets.
• Shortcut shape alignment must be handled carefully.
• BatchNorm behavior matters during training and evaluation.
Reference
He et al., Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition, CVPR 2016.

title: Inception: principle
text:
Inception: principle
Core idea
Instead of choosing one kernel size, apply multiple branches:
1 × 1,
3 × 3,
5 × 5,
pooling
then concatenate outputs along the channel dimension.
Motivation
Different objects and visual patterns may require different receptive field sizes.
Takeaway
Inception performs multi-scale feature extraction inside one module.

title: Inception: strengths and cautions
text:
Inception: strengths and cautions
Strengths
• Multi-scale feature extraction.
• Efficient use of 1 × 1 convolutions for channel reduction.
• Important historically for module-based architecture design.
Cautions
• More complex to implement and modify than plain CNNs.
• Later families such as ResNet and EfficientNet are often simpler practical
defaults.
Reference
Szegedy et al., Going Deeper with Convolutions, CVPR 2015.

title: DenseNet: principle
text:
DenseNet: principle
Core idea
Each layer receives feature maps from all previous layers:
xℓ= Hℓ([x0, x1, . . . , xℓ−1])
where [·] denotes channel-wise concatenation.
Motivation
• Encourage feature reuse.
• Improve gradient flow.
• Reduce redundant feature learning.
Takeaway
DenseNet connects layers by concatenation, while ResNet connects layers by
addition.

title: DenseNet: growth rate
text:
DenseNet: growth rate
Growth rate
If each layer adds g new channels, then after L layers:
Cout = Cin + L × g
Interpretation
• Old features are reused.
• New layers contribute only a small number of new feature maps.
• Channel dimension grows inside a dense block.
Takeaway
DenseNet controls capacity through the growth rate rather than replacing all
features at every layer.

title: DenseNet: strengths and cautions
text:
DenseNet: strengths and cautions
Strengths
• Strong feature reuse.
• Good gradient flow.
• Parameter-efficient compared with some plain deep networks.
Cautions
• Concatenation increases memory usage.
• Implementation can be less hardware-friendly than simpler blocks.

title: EfficientNet: compound scaling
text:
EfficientNet: compound scaling
Scaling rule
Given a scaling coefficient ϕ:
depth = αϕ,
width = βϕ,
resolution = γϕ
under a resource constraint.
Interpretation
• Larger models are deeper.
• Larger models are wider.
• Larger models use higher input resolution.
Takeaway
EfficientNet does not scale one axis alone; it balances all major capacity
dimensions.

EfficientNet: strengths and cautions
Strengths
• Strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

• Good transfer-learning backbone when preprocessing is respected.

• Larger variants can be memory-heavy during fine-tuning.

title: ConvNeXt: principle
text:
ConvNeXt: principle
Core idea
ConvNeXt modernizes pure CNNs using design choices inspired by
transformer-era architectures and training recipes.
Typical changes
• Larger kernel depthwise convolutions.
• Inverted bottleneck style.
• LayerNorm-style normalization in some designs.
• Fewer activation functions inside blocks.
• Modern training recipe.
Takeaway
ConvNeXt shows that carefully modernized ConvNets can remain highly
competitive.

title: ConvNeXt block: high-level view
text:
ConvNeXt block: high-level view
Simplified block
Depthwise Conv →Norm →1×1 expand →Activation →1×1 project →Residual
Design intuition
• Depthwise conv performs spatial mixing.
• Pointwise layers perform channel mixing.
• Residual connection stabilizes optimization.
• Exact details (e.g., layer scale, drop path, stem/downsample choices)
vary by implementation and checkpoint.
Takeaway
ConvNeXt combines CNN locality with modern block design

title: Why pretrained models?
text:
Why pretrained models?
Key idea
A pretrained CNN has already learned useful visual representations from a
large dataset such as ImageNet.
Benefits
• Faster convergence.
• Better performance on small or medium datasets.
• Strong baseline before designing a custom architecture.
Takeaway
For most real projects, start with a pretrained model before training from
scratch.

title: Transfer learning workflow
text:
Transfer learning workflow
Common workflow
1 Load a pretrained backbone.
2 Replace the classification head.
3 Train the new head first.
4 Optionally unfreeze part or all of the backbone.
5 Fine-tune with a smaller learning rate.
Takeaway
Fine-tuning is not only changing the last layer; it also requires a careful
training strategy.

title: Summary: CNN Architectures
text:
Summary: CNN Architectures
What to remember
• VGG: simple repeated convolutional stages.
• ResNet: residual learning for deep optimization.
• Inception: multi-scale parallel branches.
• DenseNet: dense feature reuse.
• MobileNet: efficient depthwise separable design.
• EfficientNet: compound scaling.
• ConvNeXt: modernized pure ConvNet.
Final insight
A CNN architecture is a design compromise among representation power,
optimization stability, parameter count, computation, and deployment
constraints.

title: Final practical message
text:
Final practical message
Recommended baseline strategy
• Start with ResNet-18/50 for a stable baseline.
• Try MobileNet when deployment is constrained.
• Try EfficientNet or ConvNeXt when accuracy-efficiency trade-off matters.
• Use pretrained weights and correct preprocessing whenever possible.
Final takeaway
Strong CNN practice = suitable architecture + correct preprocessing +
careful fine-tuning + honest evaluation.
